lesson.title: The Proteins That Read the Promoter: Transcription Factors
lesson.summary: Transcription factors are proteins that bind specific DNA sequences to help control whether, and how strongly, a gene is transcribed, ranging from general factors needed at every promoter to specific regulatory factors that switch individual genes on or off in particular cells.
lesson.body:
RNA polymerase, the enzyme introduced earlier that builds an mRNA copy of a gene, does not act alone in eukaryotic cells. Especially at the promoters used by RNA polymerase II, the polymerase that transcribes protein coding genes, it depends on a set of helper proteins called transcription factors to find the right starting point and to have any meaningful influence over how much transcription actually occurs. A transcription factor is a protein, like any other, built from a sequence of amino acids folded into a specific three dimensional shape, but its defining feature is a region called a DNA-binding domain that recognizes and binds a particular short DNA sequence, along with a separate region, often called an activation or repression domain, that interacts with other proteins to influence transcription once the factor is bound.

Transcription factors fall into two broad categories. General transcription factors are required at the core promoter of essentially every gene RNA polymerase II transcribes; they help position the polymerase correctly and open the DNA there so transcription can begin at all. On their own, general transcription factors and RNA polymerase support only a low, basal rate of transcription. Specific, or regulatory, transcription factors are different: each one recognizes a particular DNA sequence found only in the regulatory regions of particular genes, such as an enhancer or a promoter-proximal element, and by binding there it either increases transcription, acting as an activator, or decreases it, acting as a repressor, of that specific gene. Because different cell types express different sets of specific transcription factors, the same gene can be strongly activated in one cell type and left alone, or actively repressed, in another, which is the molecular basis for the cell type specific and combinatorial control described in the previous chapter.

Activator transcription factors bound at an enhancer, even one located far from the promoter, can influence transcription there because the DNA between the two sites loops around, bringing the activator into contact, often through a large multiprotein bridge called Mediator, with RNA polymerase and the general transcription factors assembled at the promoter, stabilizing that assembly and increasing the rate at which new transcripts are initiated. Repressor transcription factors can work in more than one way: some simply block an activator from binding nearby, some directly interfere with assembly of the polymerase machinery at the promoter, and some recruit proteins that modify chromatin to make it more tightly packed and less accessible at that gene, connecting back to the chromatin based regulation covered in the previous chapter.

A transcription factor's own activity is frequently regulated as well, so that it only turns its target genes on or off in response to an appropriate signal. Some transcription factors sit in the cytoplasm, inactive, until a specific signaling molecule binds them and triggers their movement into the nucleus. Others require a chemical modification, such as the addition of a phosphate group by a signaling enzyme, before they can bind DNA or interact effectively with the transcription machinery. This adds one more layer to the overall picture built across this unit: whether, and how strongly, a given gene is transcribed in a given cell at a given moment depends on the combined state of its chromatin packaging and the particular set of transcription factors that are both present and active there, binding DNA sequences that ultimately determine whether RNA polymerase gets to work.
